en: Preface to the Commentary on the Perfect Penetration of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, Volume One, Part One,
composed by the Śramaṇa Chuandeng of Youxi at Mount Tiantai.
An Account of the Origins.

I have long desired to compose this commentary. In the Xinchou year of the Wanli era, I attended the invitation of the lay practitioner Yu Sishun De-yuan at Shengguo Temple in Hulin for the Lotus Samādhi retreat. There, the assembled fellow practitioners requested that I produce this work.
I previously composed a preface titled *The Commentary on Perfect Penetration* (*Yuántōng shū*). It has been delayed until now, and I have not yet fulfilled my original intention.
This autumn, the lay practitioner Wang Bo’wu of Linhai visited me at Youxi, and together with the bhikṣu [name missing], he made this request.
Furthermore, ten people have joined together to [make this request].
I sought the Bodhisattva Mahākaruṇā, who silently bestowed her transformative empowerment.
For seven days, I took the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing as my primary practice;
yet, although I did not receive a manifest response, it was as if, within the profound darkness, his refined mind secretly and swiftly awakened my spiritual consciousness. It was here that...
Having attained some degree of awakening through the Sāgaramudrā-samādhi, the lay practitioner Yang Haiweng recently visited me in the mountains.
He presented me with a portrait titled "The Radiance of the Sāgaramudrā," which resonated deeply with my own mind.
Consequently, I wished to change the title of this commentary to *Sāgaramudrā-samādhi*. However, both the bhikṣus and the lay practitioners said, "Ten years ago, [this was already...]"

In composing this preface, it seems as though there is something being awaited. Moreover, since the primary tenet of this sutra is perfect penetration (yuantong), I pray that you do not alter it further.

Would it not be appropriate to use this title for the *Lengyan Xingfa* (The Practice of the Śūraṅgama)? This is because, in the coming autumn at my mountain retreat, there will be a formal ritual for the Śūraṅgama altar.
Thus I have spoken these words, yet I shall still title it the *Yuantong Shu* (Commentary on Perfect Penetration).
Preface: I received the Master’s teachings from the Great Monk Baishong. Regarding the essential purport of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he had many further insights and elucidations.
In the tenth year of the Wanli era, the year being Renwu, the Master was lecturing on this sūtra at Shengshui in Tiantai. One day...
Upon entering the room, it was empty and devoid of anyone. I joined my palms, knelt with my knees touching, and requested the essential meaning of Great Samādhi.
The Master merely stared intently around him, remaining silent without uttering a word. At that very moment, I experienced a profound awakening.
I practiced according to this for a long time until the year of Dinghai (1647), when I first composed the *Xuan Yi* (Profound Meaning) in four fascicles at the Youxi Monastery in Tiantai.
I have lodged this intention within the "Chapter on the Substance and the Principle" (*Tizong Zhang*) to benefit others, hoping thereby to repay even slightly the kindness of the Dharma-milk.
I had previously believed that among the masters of antiquity and today, none had ever revealed its profound mysteries.

However, upon later reading the *Combined Commentary* by the Great Master Jiyin, as well as having obtained the book *Zhengmai* last autumn, I found that both extensively elucidate the manifestation of the nature of seeing.
Because I have understood the point where the minds meet, our views accord without prior agreement; from the beginning, there has been no gap between the ancient and the modern.

I regret that the *He lun* (Compendium) is concise yet not comprehensive, and that the *Zhengmai* (Orthodox Pulse) is prolix yet loses its foundation. Regarding the meaning of the "Middle Way," there remains something to await future sages;

how could it be fully exhausted by my own meager ignorance? Nevertheless, like a leopard glimpsed through a tube, I have seen one aspect of it, and I cannot but share this with those who have not yet [attained it].
This is the explanation of one who peers [into the depths]. A person of great capacity possesses a comprehensive vision; may those who have seen the whole leopard not deign to censure me.

Herein, I shall reconcile the similarities and differences between this sutra and other sutras—those where the names and meanings are identical yet the underlying intent differs. First, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*.
This is so. There are cases where the names differ but the meaning and intent are identical; the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is an example.

There are cases where the names differ and the meaning is the same, yet the intent differs; the *Lotus Sūtra* is an example. There are cases where the names differ and both the meaning and intent are identical, such that they cannot be categorized together;
the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* is an example. Furthermore, there are cases where the phrasing is identical but the meaning and intent differ, being as far apart as heaven and earth.
This refers to Zhuangzi. Indeed, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* shares the same meaning as "distinguishing through vigorous characteristics.
However, that [sūtra] was spoken solely for bodhisattvas of deep stages who emerge from the provisional and enter the middle; thus, the Buddha told the Bodhisattva Resolute Mind (*Dṛḍhamati*).
The Śūraṅgama Samādhi cannot be attained by Bodhisattvas of the first stage and so forth; only those of the tenth stage can attain it.
It enumerates one hundred kinds of samādhi: first, cultivating the mind so that it is like empty space;
second, observing the various minds of present sentient beings—the initial mind being that which can be cultivated; and third, discerning the various faculties of sentient beings.

Regarding the sharp and dull [faculties]: the fourth [chapter] definitively understands that sentient beings’ causes and effects proceed from the past until the hundredth [chapter], where they enter the Great Parinirvāṇa without being eternally extinguished;
all of these are severed from the initial resolve. Is this not a case where the names and meanings are the same, yet the underlying intent differs?

If we consider the *Awakening of Full Enlightenment* (*Yuánjué*) as a sūtra, although the names differ, "Full Enlightenment" (*yuánjué*) is identical to "Perfect Penetration" (*yuántōng*), as both equally expound a single principle. As for "Luxuriance" (*shē...*)— (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a commentary on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, specifically discussing the relationship between different titles and their underlying meaning.)

The three names, *samatha* and so forth, all expound the same single practice; however, the names and characteristics discussed therein appear and disappear differently, and their detailed and abbreviated expositions vary.

Indeed, without mastery of the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, one cannot cultivate the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*; and without mastery of the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, one cannot cultivate the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*.
Students should therefore study these two sutras in conjunction with one another. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and this sutra share the same meaning.

Regarding the distinctiveness of the "intention": the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (jñāna-darśana) throughout the various teachings of his lifetime were established as a whole for the sake of the *Lotus Sūtra*’s revelation of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
However, it is the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* alone that most intimately clarifies this Buddha-knowledge and vision; thus, it is said that the intention is distinct.
Although the *Lotus Sūtra* states that the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, for the sake of the great causal conditions, reveal, cause to awaken to, and enter into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision...

In the initial passages of the sutra, not a single word has ever been seen that refers to this meaning. This is because it lies within the *intention* (*yi*), yet its meaning has not been explicitly articulated.
What is meant by "intention"? It is the fundamental resolve of the Buddha. What is meant by "fundamental resolve"? It is the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*).
Indeed, the Buddha appeared in the world primarily for the sake of this matter. However, as sentient beings’ capacities were not yet sufficient, he was compelled to [proceed otherwise].
The single reality-mark (dharmatā) is explained through the distinct enumeration of the ten realms; within the single Buddha-vehicle, there is explained the differentiation of the five vehicles.
Although the nine realms are displayed, the underlying intent does not reside in those nine. People do not understand this intent and each clings to their own position; thus, their visions differ.
Even if a bodhisattva were to perceive the marks of the true recompense and adornment, they might still say that it does not fully satisfy their original aspiration.

Although it is said that there are five vehicles, the underlying intention does not reside in the five. People do not understand this intention and each insists upon the different path they have entered.
Even if sentient beings were to achieve the bodhisattva path, one could say that their original aspiration has not been fully realized.

In some cases, the great is separated from the small (*Avataṃsaka*). In others, the great is not utilized (*Āgama*). In others, one hears of the great but realizes the small (*Vaipulya* and *Prajñāpāramitā*).
Or, one hears of the small but realizes the great (*Āgama*). Or, they know each other (*Aniyata*). Or, they do not know each other (*Guhyaka*).
None of these represent the Buddha’s true intention; it may be said that they fail to fully express his original intent. Even if other sūtras possess textual and doctrinal richness...
If the *Lotus Sūtra* does not discuss the Buddha’s intention, it may indeed be said that it fails to fully express his original aspiration.
For the Buddha’s intention lies in having all beings sit together on one seat and share the flavor of a single path; with the rain of this one flavor, he nourishes both humans and flowers.

As it is said, there is neither small nor great; all return to the Dharma-realm, and only after every person has attained Buddhahood will his purpose be fulfilled. He speaks clearly and explicitly, desiring to...
Is it not here that sentient beings are revealed, awakened, and led into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision?

Therefore, while the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* share the same meaning but differ in their intent, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* and this sutra share both the same meaning and intent; yet they cannot be treated as identical categories.
The eternally abiding true mind discussed in this sutra shares with the four types of restraint the same intent as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* in upholding the rules (*vinaya*) while discussing the eternal.

However, there are cases where both the literal expression and the underlying meaning are general, yet they are categorized under a specific heading; these examples are fully explained below in the section on "Characteristics of the Teaching.

One must not treat them as being of the same class. Regarding instances where the names in this sutra coincide with those in the *Zhuangzi*, such as the "Two Volumes" and the "Pointing Out the Finger," [the details are as follows].
It is not the finger. How could four fascicles rely on arduous toil to achieve the realization of the subtle and essential?

When the Venerable Fang transcribed this sutra by dictation, he used the characters of this region to polish its expression; however, while the words are the same, their meaning and intent are different.
This is because in this sutra, the tree can be pointed out, yet the seeing cannot be pointed out. Where pointing is always seeing and there is no tree, pointing is always the tree and...

Those who hold such views do so because they remain mired in delusion and are unable to simultaneously dissolve both "is" and "is not. Consequently, there arises the distinction between what can be pointed out and what cannot.

If, however, one relies upon this true, essential, wondrously enlightened, and luminous nature, then "is" and "is not" are simultaneously dissolved, and both "pointing" and "not pointing" are forgotten.
Thus, one is able to transcend both pointing and not pointing. That *Qi wu lun* (Treatise on the Equalization of Things) speaks of worldly "is" and "is not," all of which arise from...
This and that arise in succession; the sages do not follow them. To illuminate them from the perspective of Heaven, it is also because of this.
This is that, and that is also this. That has its own right and wrong, and this has its own right and wrong. Is there, then, truly such a thing as "that being right"?
Or is there truly no such thing as "that being right"? When "that" and "right" cannot find their counterparts, we call this the Pivot of the Dao. The Pivot begins...
To find the center of the ring is to respond to the infinite; thus, "is" is also infinite, and "is not" is also infinite. Therefore it is said: nothing is better than clarity.

Only then can one bring forth illumination. For this reason, it is said that using a finger to illustrate that a finger is not a finger is not as good as using what is not a finger to illustrate that a finger is not a finger;
using a horse to illustrate that a horse is not a horse—[is not as good as using what is not a horse to illustrate that a horse is not a horse].
A horse is not like using "non-horse" as a metaphor for the horse being non-horse. Heaven and earth are but a single finger; the myriad things are but a single horse.
Zhuangzi likely held that what is right for them is precisely what is right for me.

It is only because people refuse to measure others by themselves and cling to the notion of a self, resolutely deciding that they are right and others are wrong, that public opinion remains so discordant. This is the primary cause.

For this reason, one uses one’s own finger as a metaphor for the finger that is not a finger. Thus, while my finger may be "is," it is not permissible to use it as a metaphor for another person’s finger being "not.
If one does not realize that the other person’s finger is also a finger, how can one conclude that it is not a finger simply because it is not in one’s own hand?
It would be better to turn back and examine it from the perspective of that other person. If the other were to speak thus:
One might also say that what I call a finger is not a finger. Thus, through such reciprocal explanations between "self" and "other," both parties are equally self-righteous and mutually condemnatory.
Is there, then, truly something that is right? Or is there truly something that is wrong?
Yet, one sees only that there is nothing that is right and nothing that is not right; thus, right and wrong are extinguished therein. The analogy of "horse" and "not-horse" is likewise.
It is so. This is precisely what that [text] calls the "Heaven within the Ring" which is impartial toward both right and wrong, namely the Pivot of the Way (*dao-ju*).
To trace its fundamental principle, it is simply the One Qi. How does this compare to the present sutra’s teaching on the wondrously pure and luminous essence of Bodhi?

It states that the seeing and the conditions for seeing, along with all perceived forms, are like flowers in the sky—fundamentally non-existent. How could there be right or wrong therein? The difference is more than that between heaven and earth.

How vast is the difference between these two! The words concerning the "sinews and knots" clarify the master of nourishing life; therefore, [the text] cites the butcher Ding’s dissection of an ox to illustrate this.
When I first began my work of dissection, all that I saw was nothing but the ox. After three years, I have never again seen a whole ox.
At the present time, I encounter it with the spirit rather than looking with the eyes; my sensory faculties [are stilled].

He rested while his spirit desired to move. He relied upon the natural principles of Heaven; he split the great cavities and guided [his blade] through the great apertures, following their inherent nature.
He had never even touched the sinews or the ligaments, much less the large joints. Such was the intention of Cook Ding: he spoke of the Way that he loved, not of mere skill.
When skill advances to refinement, it reaches the state of spontaneity, where one does not even know how it is so. Then—

One must not designate this by the name of "skill," but rather by the name of "the Way" (*dào*). When he first began learning to butcher oxen, everything his eyes beheld was nothing but the ox itself.
After three years, however, he saw the sinews, veins, bones, and joints, each with its own empty spaces through which his blade could glide effortlessly;
he no longer saw it as a whole ox, and so forth. This is a metaphor for when one first begins to study the Way.
In the affairs of the human world, one cannot see through them nor penetrate them; one sees only all matters entangled and pressing, unable to extricate oneself.

Once one's practice has become mature, however, one perceives that each matter possesses its own principle and that these principles are inherently so; one then responds to them with pure consistency.
Great and small alike, none require any exertion. What is this Way? It is the master of nourishing life.
When the study of the Way of nourishing life reaches this point, it may be considered perfected.

Yet, compared to the Way of Bodhi in this sutra, when one reaches such purity and is able to fully comprehend that both the seer and the conditions of seeing, as well as all perceived forms, are like flowers in the sky, fundamentally non-existent—[this former path] cannot compare.
All things, as they encounter conditions and confront objects, are of one and the same flavor of the Dharma-body; therefore it is said:
"If you merely do not follow after the three kinds of continuous succession of worldly discrimination, then because the three conditions are severed, the three causes will not arise.
Thus, the madness of your own *Yajñadatta* within your mind will naturally subside. This subsiding is itself Bodhi; it is not obtained from others. Why rely on arduous toil or painful effort?"
Cultivation and realization—this is precisely what Perfect Enlightenment (Zhengyuan Jue) means by "abiding at all times without giving rise to deluded thoughts.
How could it rely upon arduous toil or the slightest effort? This is what the ancient masters meant when they said, "One employs the words but does not grasp their [superficial] meaning.

In recent times, many who propagate the sutras have failed to understand this point; some even compare the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* to the *Zhuangzi* and the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* to the works of Laozi. There is no... [end of fragment].

How strange! To rely on oral commentaries and transcribed notes, claiming that the Buddha’s entire Great Canon was all produced from within the *Zhuangzi*—having already discarded gold to carry hemp, one now recognizes the hemp as gold. Is this not lamentable?

The practice of clarifying the structural divisions (*kepan*) of Buddhist scriptures began with the Dharma Master Dao’an of the Western Jin dynasty. He maintained that regardless of whether a scripture belongs to the Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna, it can all be divided into three parts:
the introduction (*nidāna*), the main body (*saddharma*), and the dissemination (*pariṇāmanā*). The introduction then narrates the circumstances of a given scripture.
As for the "Causes and Conditions": regarding the "Correctness," it means that the correct exposition brings benefit to those who encounter it;

regarding the "Circulation," it means entrusting disciples to propagate [the teaching] so that devas and nāgas will provide protection, ensuring that the waters of the sublime Dharma flow from this day forward and that the tools for understanding the holy teachings remain unobstructed in future generations.
Within these three parts, I have divided the text into sections according to the beginning and end of each thematic meaning—what is known as the "division like rice stalks."
Just as a tree has branches to contain its trunk and roots, and water has sources from which its tributaries flow, the ancients said that "sections" (ke) encompass great meaning;
this is indeed not false. Therefore, when various masters comment on the sutras, they invariably divide them into sections.
For instance, regarding the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, masters such as those of Wuxing, Wenling, Changshui, and Gushan all established their own sectional divisions (*kepan*), yet Tianru alone...
I have resolved to eliminate them. However, while "no division" (wu ke) is beneficial solely for those of superior capacity, "having divisions" (you ke) provides benefit to those of lesser ability.

Furthermore, when a beginner encounters a scripture with many divisions, they become overwhelmed, like one gazing out at the vast ocean; yet after long practice, having mastered the classification of sections, they move through it with ease, like a blade gliding through a whetstone.

Thus, the classification of scriptures is also a matter of essential importance. If one allows fine subdivisions to rise like smoke and miscellaneous arguments to fly like dust, the discourse will flow on endlessly and boundlessly, becoming so profound that it can never be fully investigated.
This is what Tiantai did not permit and what Wēnlíng deeply criticized. Although I am not quick-witted, how could I dare not be cautious?
Now, following the major topical divisions of Master Gūshān, I have further revised and refined them; I have structured the text according to the *Huìjiě* (Comprehensive Explanation).
This is intended to facilitate mastery; by following the main text while arranging sub-sections alongside it, one does not lose the structural integrity of the chapters.

Therefore, the "Mother" sections are written above and the "Child" sections are listed at the side—hence they are called "side-sections" (*pángkē*). Those who have long practiced in lecture halls may retain them when using the text, and omit them when setting it aside.
These meticulous insect-like characters are as fine as silk threads; truly, they will pose no obstacle to the Dharma-eye.

Some suspect that this sutra was slandered [as spurious], yet it was personally proclaimed by the Tathāgata’s golden mouth and kept secret in the land of India. It was only during the Shénlóng era of the Great Táng dynasty that it first reached Zhōnag.
Furthermore, the Great Master Zhìzhě of Tiāntái was born during the Liáng dynasty of the Xiāo clan; he attained the Way and preached the Dharma during the Chén dynasty.
During the Sui dynasty, it was heard in advance that there existed in India the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*. [The Master] considered it to be perfectly harmonious and comprehensive;
thus, he gazed toward the West for eighteen years. Although he did not live to see it, the dharma-gates of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* he established largely corresponded in advance with its teachings.

For instance, his "three types of cessation" correspond to the three dharmas such as *śamatha*, and his dharma-gate of the "inherent nature" corresponds to the seven elements of the true nature of form.
The union with emptiness and so forth clarifies the stages of the path (bhūmi), which corresponds to the fifty-five positions of the true path to Bodhi.
The ten objects, three obstructions, and four demons correspond to the fifty layers of the objective realms of the aggregates (skandha). As for the citation from the *Aṅgulimālīya Sūtra*, it states:
"That eye-faculty [perceives] all Tathāgatas as eternally present, seeing them with perfect clarity; it is fully endowed and without deficiency. This applies to all six faculties.
Thus it is said. This clarifies that the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—the perfect cultivation of the Great Samādhi—is a single illumination of the fundamental nature;
it is not something accomplished through artificial cultivation. This accords with the ten points on the nature of seeing, such as the "fingertip moving the light" analogy.

For this reason, since ancient times, no masters have failed to rely upon the Tiantai teachings to expound the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. Such is the case for the various masters of Gushan, Wuxing, Boting, and Tongjiang, who were indeed [the successors of this tradition].

From the patriarchal descendants down to Changshui, and from the founder of our own school, Xianshou, to Wenglun—who was originally of the Chan school—they have never failed to honor and employ [these teachings], for the *śamatha-vipaśyanā* method is the essential meaning of the sūtras taught by the World-Honored Buddhas of antiquity.
As for Tianru’s *Huìjiě*, it draws even more extensively from these sources; it is only in recent times that scholastic studies have become diluted.
This is particularly egregious. Having a penchant for the new and a preference for the extraordinary, he further rejects what is common and aligns himself with what is divergent.

Because it is said that although Ānanda requested three methods, the Tathāgata replied only with "one mind," he consequently rejects the three types of cessation (*śamatha*) and finds them entirely unacceptable.

This stems from his failure to understand that the stimulus and the response correspond to one another, and that the sounding block and the mallet strike each other in turn; thus, at the point of questioning, the names of the three cessations were fully extended.
In response, I shall briefly expound the meaning of the three types of cessation (*śamatha*).

If one can first study the three cessations of Tiantai and further master the three contemplations (*vipaśyanā*) of the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*), then by using those to read this, the three dharmas of the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi* will be as clear as pointing at one's own palm.
Teachers such as these are as numerous as rice, hemp, bamboo, and reeds; how could I possibly enumerate their errors in detail? It is only regarding one or two teachers of recent times that—
These [errors] are manifested in his brushwork and further brought calamity upon the wooden printing blocks. If they are not refuted and rejected, they will greatly obstruct the Way.

However, it is impossible to examine and investigate every single instance of their fallacy; therefore, I shall refute only the opening of the array, and the remainder shall naturally yield to the wind.
The *Lengyan bieyan* says: "If one relies on the three types of cessation (*śamatha*) to practice, it is like lashing a boat against a mooring stake;
there is only this single sword of the Vajra King, which destroys existence upon contact and shatters emptiness upon being aimed at. And so forth.
Seolbang said: "While it is true that one cannot moor a ship with a single stake, neither can one proceed without an oar.
An 'oar' refers to the three kinds of cessation (*tri-śamatha*). What matters is how the one who rows performs.
To speak of times of peace, even the Vajra King’s precious sword must be stored high on a shelf; yet now, our King has been invaded by rebels."
He employs troops to eliminate them; he holds to these five desires to punish the violent and rebellious. Try turning back and questioning him: when contact exists, existence perishes;
when one aims for emptiness, emptiness fails. What, then, is this thing? I laughed at this master, who was not skilled at stealing; he was much like someone covering his ears while stealing a bell.
One must know that that which subsumes all things and remains cool and clear is True Emptiness (*śūnyatā*); that which illuminates the mass of darkness and shines alone is... [the luminous wisdom].

Śamatha is that which establishes the myriad dharmas yet leaves no trace; it is the wondrous existence. Samādhi is that which transcends all burdens yet responds perfectly; it is the threefold samādhi.
The Middle Way is that which unifies existence and non-existence while remaining wondrously absolute. It is that which dwells in quiescent extinction yet possesses universal knowledge.
It is dhyāna. It is eternally one yet three; emptiness is permissible, the provisional is permissible, and the middle is permissible. It is eternally three yet one.

I do not know which is emptiness, which is the provisional, and which is the middle. To cultivate in this manner is called the Wondrous Lotus, the Vajra-King Jewel-Awakening, the Illusion-like Samādhi, and the True Samādhi of the Buddha-Mother. This is the Buddha’s...
Knowledge and vision. The *Haiyin faguang* (Ocean-Seal Radiance) was spoken by the Tathāgata in the past; the wise have elucidated it in subsequent ages;
the wise reveal it in the present. Two sutras have sealed it since antiquity. One Buddha and one Patriarch transmit mind-to-mind.
To be able to follow this is to continue the life-force of the Buddha’s wisdom. To slander this is to sever the seeds of the Buddha among humanity. It may be said:
How uncautious! How can one not be cautious?

Lately, the *Zhengmai* (Correct Pulse) of the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra* has greatly deviated from the *Huìjiě* (Commentary and Explanation) by Chan Master Tiānrú; consequently, this error has even spread to the Tiantai tradition.

Since all the various masters have employed the three types of cessation (*tri-śamatha*) from the Tiantai tradition to interpret the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, and since Tianru— having synthesized these various interpretations—
established them as his own school’s discourse, he could not help but align his own realization of the heart-essence (*citta-tattva*) with that of Tiantai.
Now, wishing to clear the calumny against Tiantai, one cannot but act for Tianru and for the various masters.
To clarify this, Zhengmei says:
"I shall now briefly set forth three points to reveal the general meaning. The first is various types of inconsistencies in confusion;
this further has two parts. The first is inconsistency in question and answer, referring to Ānanda’s initial inquiry regarding *śamatha*."
Regarding "samādhi-dhyāna," various masters have predominantly explained it by means of the three types of cessation (*tri-śamatha*) from the Tiantai school.

Furthermore, when the Tathāgata observes the capacities of his audience, his questions and answers must correspond to one another. If Ānanda’s current question were indeed about the three cessations of the Tiantai school, then the meaning of the Tathāgata’s subsequent response would necessarily correspond to the practice of those three cessations.
Yet, the commentators still point toward the [textual] "knotting" (*granthi*); where [is this to be found]?
This is the "stopping by realizing the true essence" (*tǐzhēn zhǐ*). Wherein lies the "stopping that follows conditions through skillful means" (*fāngbiàn suíyuán zhǐ*)?

And wherein lies the "stopping that quiets the discrimination of the two extremes" (*xī èrbiān fēnbié zhǐ*)? Now, upon carefully examining the scriptural text, there is not a single trace of such meanings or characteristics. Furthermore, the commentators do not further reconcile these points with the preceding questions.
As for the various passages that investigate the mind and reveal the seeing-nature (*xiànjiàn*), they likewise do not clarify how these relate to the three types of stopping.
As for this passage: "How could the question concern the three *śamatha* [stages] as being the original source, while the answer is entirely inconsistent?
This would mean that the Tathāgata answered the point of inquiry erroneously; how then can it be considered a teaching that discerns the capacities of beings?

Furthermore, even if what the Tathāgata answered were entirely consistent with the three *śamatha*, it would still fall within the errors identified by Tiantai, because he explicitly stated that *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are partial."

To take this [view] is like having only a single wheel or a solitary wing; one cannot travel far. How could the questions and answers in the Buddhist assemblies have emerged from beneath the teachings of Tiantai?
This is an even more extreme form of irrationality.

Xuemo slandered him, saying: "When I first encountered the *Zhengmo* (Correct Pulse), which enters into the commentaries on the sutra and expounds the ten kinds of seeing one's nature within the first two fascicles, I highly praised its insight as surpassing that of the ten ancient masters and marveled at its truly grand strategic vision.

However, upon reading the *Xuánjiě* (Profound Explanation), which greatly subverts the teachings of the Tiantai school regarding the three stages of cessation (*sanzhi*), I realized that regarding this sutra, [the author] was merely peering through a tube."

As for the leopard, one sees but a single stripe; yet regarding the establishment of tenets and the transmission of the teachings by various schools—such as the principles of "ascending the hall" and "entering the room"—how are they any different from a yellow-mouthed infant who, pretending to learn like an adult, engages in grandiloquent and far-fetched discourse? When those with discernment observe this from the sidelines, how laughable it is!
Now, I shall refute this in two sections. First, I shall refute the two points where the question and answer are inconsistent. First, I present them:
Next is the third type of cessation. Next, the three types of cessation according to the Perfect and Sudden teaching are clarified; only then will the text be analyzed and matched accordingly.
Regarding the third type of cessation, first is "Cessation that Embodies Reality": All phenomena arise from conditions; causes and conditions are empty and without a master.

To still the mind and reach the fundamental source is why one is called a *śramaṇa*. Knowing that causes and conditions are a provisional confluence and that their illusory nature is void, it is therefore termed "embodiment."

Discursive thoughts that grasp at objects cease as soon as emptiness is realized; emptiness itself is the truth. Therefore, this is called "stopping by realizing the truth. Second is "stopping by following conditions through skillful means.

If those of the Two Vehicles were to realize the truth, they would have no need for skillful means; however, when Bodhisattvas enter the realm of the provisional, it is precisely here that they should apply their practice.
Knowing that emptiness is not [inherently] empty is called "skillful means" (*upāya*). Discerning the medicine according to the illness is called "following conditions" (*pratyaya*).

When the mind rests in conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it is called "calm abiding" (*śamatha*). As the Sūtra says, "Whether moving or resting, the mind is always one"—this also serves to verify this meaning.

To distinguish between the three cessations and the three extremes—namely, the flux of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) and the fixed reliance on nirvana (*nirvāṇa*)—is all partial practice; it does not accord with the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*).

Now, one knows that the mundane is not mundane; at the limit of the mundane, there is stillness. Nor is the non-mundane attained; at the limit of emptiness, there is stillness. This is called "resting from the two extremes.
As for the characteristics of Perfect and Sudden Calm Abiding and Insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*): when calm abiding takes the Truths as its object, then one Truth is three Truths;
when the Truths are bound to calm abiding, then one calm abiding is three calm abidings. It is like the three marks [of existence], which reside within a single moment of mind; though they are one...
Regarding the mind of mindfulness, there are three aspects (and so forth). What are these aspects? The essence of ignorance and inversion is precisely the reality of the true mark;

this is called "True Cessation of the Essence. This true mark pervades all places; as it encounters conditions and passes through objects, the mind remains unmoved—this is called "Expedient Cessation Following Conditions.
Birth-and-death and nirvana, stillness and dispersion, come to rest—this is called "Cessation of the Two Extremes."

The analysis of the extremes regarding cessation is concluded; the brief exposition of the texts on cessation and contemplation is finished. Now, I shall correlate these sections with the corresponding passages of the sutra.

From the first fascicle, where the mind is investigated in seven locations, up to the second fascicle, where it says, "When seeing the seer, that which sees is not the seer," this is the Tathāgata’s response to Ānanda’s question concerning *śamatha* (cessation).

This corresponds to the Tiantai concept of "cessation through realizing the true nature" (*tǐzhēn zhǐ*). This correlation continues up to the third fascicle, where the [nature of] clarity is explained.
"Regarding the cessation of the aggregates, bases, and elements," he replied, "it is *samādhi*; this refers to the cessation through following conditions by means of skillful means.

Up to this point, it clarifies that the seven great elements are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha. He replied, "It is *dhyāna*; this refers to the cessation through stilling the discrimination of the two extremes.

For cessation does not cease of itself; cessation is accomplished by means of the illumination of the truths. Cultivation does not cultivate of itself; cultivation is accomplished by means of the nature of understanding. This resides within the Tathāgata..."
The answer was as follows: It was originally based on the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of purity and luminosity, to open up Ānanda’s understanding of the three truths (*trisatya*).

At the point where Ānanda followed his hearing and entered contemplation, he took the very nature of these three truths to accomplish the cultivation of the three types of cessation (*śamatha*), such as *śamatha* itself.
Thus, the truths and the contemplations are like form and sound, or shadow and echo; they must necessarily proceed in mutual dependence.
Regarding this sutra and the dharma-gate of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, if various masters do not fall into doubt, they will instead give rise to slander.
This is precisely because they fail to understand the distinction between the objects of cultivation and contemplation, as well as their mutually supportive relationship.
This is a great malady for those who study the Buddha-way; therefore, the sutras frequently speak of the path of *śamatha*, the path of wondrous bodhi, and wondrous adornment.
The "road" refers to the nature (*dharmatā*), the objects (*ālambana*), and the truths (*satya*); it is like a broad, level highway.

*Śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are the dharma-gates capable of cultivation; they are like the person traveling the road. Thus, even in the *Huìjiě* (Commentary on the Meaning), it has never been said otherwise.
As Guishan’s commentary explains: "Although Ānanda made his request based on the Great Samādhi, there is no separate method for it shown by the Tathāgata in the subsequent text.

From the initial discernment of the true and the false, through the subsequent harmonization of the true and the false, up until the fourth fascicle, all serves only to elucidate the Perfect Principle (*yuanli*). Indeed, this Perfect Principle is the very essence of the Great Samādhi."
This is the fundamental point. In this way, it may also be said that this clearly indicates the meaning of the mutual necessity of the object (*viṣaya*) and contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

Yet, when Jiaoguang read the *Huìjiě* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning), he did so solely out of a sense of his own correctness, while disparaging others; why is it that he failed to even taste or consider such principles?
Now, I shall further provide a clear explanation and correlation with the Three Truths (*trisatya*) to clarify the meaning of the three types of cessation (*trividha-śamatha*). [From the] Sūtra...

At the beginning of the text, seven points are used to investigate the deluded mind and show it has no location; next, three points are used to investigate the deluded mind and show it has no substance.
This explicitly refutes the deluded mind while implicitly revealing the true mind. Next, the faculty of seeing is integrated back into the mind, and the true seeing is clarified through ten meanings.
This incidentally refutes false seeing and correctly reveals true seeing. In terms of the Three Truths, this is the Truth of Reality (*paramārtha-satya*). It is indeed profound stillness and purity.
Purity is called the True. To bring all phenomena together and return them to oneself is called the True.
To point directly at the nature that is neither born nor extinguished, without involving the myriad distinctions, is called the True.

Causing Ānanda to realize this immediately, so that he does not fall into discrimination nor remain caught in verbal explanations, is called "substance" (tǐ). His mind becoming serene and transcendent is called "stopping" (zhǐ). This is not merely the substance of the True.
Why do you stop there? Yet, the Tathāgata did not fail to speak of the meaning of realizing the essence.

As it is said: "When I do not see," and again, "at the time of seeing-seeing. It is also said: "If one can transform things"—such instances of the intent behind realizing the essence are more than sufficient.

How could human desires for doubt and slander compare with the intimacy and clarity of the scriptural text? Now, let us further interpret this by correlating it with the three contemplations of the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*).
It says: "If bodhisattvas awaken to the stillness of perfect enlightenment and, with a mind of pure awakening, take stillness as their practice—stillness is the truth.
To 'take stillness' is the meaning of embodying it. The scripture clearly explains the aggregates (*skandha*), sense bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).

The realm (*dhātu*) is the original *tathāgatagarbha*. To speak of it in terms of the two truths, it is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). This is because it is not separated from the myriad categories of phenomena;

that which is examined and verified in each and every instance is called "conventional. By causing Ānanda to experience various conditions and confront objects, and by having him extend his understanding through analogy, he perceives the *tathāgatagarbha* within each and every one of these phenomena—this is called "skillful means following conditions. Thus, regarding all these phenomena, he rests his mind in non-attachment.

Movement is called stillness. This has two meanings. First, it is the practice of Bodhisattvas at the profound stages, which is identical to the "contemplation of the provisional" (*jia-guan*) in the *Śrī-mālā-devī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*.
It consists of knowing the illness and identifying the medicine, then administering the medicine according to the illness so that it may be ingested and practiced.

Second, it is the practice of those with the initial resolve, which is identical to the "samādhi" in the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*). That sūtra says: "If Bodhisattvas awaken to pure, perfect enlightenment..."
By means of the mind of stillness and awakening, one knows that the nature of the mind, as well as the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*), all arise from illusory transformations.
Thus, one gives rise to various illusions in order to eliminate the illusionist; by transforming these illusions, one brings liberation to the illusory multitude.

The nature of the mind, the sense organs, and their objects are precisely what this sutra refers to as the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*). Since they all arise from illusory transformations, they share the same meaning as the metaphor of "empty flowers" found in the section on the five aggregates. That is to say:

"Arising all illusions" refers to the skillful means of cessation in accordance with conditions. "Using that which removes illusion" refers to the skillful means of ceasing the delusions to be eliminated.
"Transforming all illusions to enlighten the illusory multitudes" means that one who cultivates this cessation can transform the defiled aggregates and realms to achieve pure aggregates and realms.
At the initial stage, one first cultivates the contemplation of illusion to enlighten and transform the multitudes of their own inherent nature.
Having thus arisen, one then employs these skillful means to transform sentient beings in other realms.

The scripture clarifies that the seven great elements are true emptiness in their nature, and that this true emptiness in nature is true form. To express this in terms of the Three Truths, it refers to the Middle Truth (*madhyama-satya*).
For that which governs all phenomena and exercises sovereign mastery is called the "Middle"; that which is neither biased nor leaning, pervading the entire dharma-realm, is called the... [Middle].
In the midst [of this], cause Ānanda to clearly perceive this nature so that he does not form interpretations of it as either empty or existent.
To enter directly into the very center of the center is called "stopping the discrimination of the two extremes. The *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* says:

"If bodhisattvas awaken to pure, perfect enlightenment, they use their mind of quiescent awakening to refrain from grasping at illusory transformations or various signs of stillness. They understand that both body and mind are entirely obstructive and devoid of cognition."
Awakened clarity does not rely on various obstructions; it forever attains transcendence over the realms of both obstruction and non-obstruction.

It experiences the world, as well as body and mind, while their characteristics reside within the sensory domains. Just as one knows that the resonance of a bell within a vessel issues forth to the exterior, it does not grasp at illusory transformations or various states of stillness;
this is the cessation of dualistic discrimination. Forever attaining transcendence over the realms of obstruction and non-obstruction, it comes to rest.

This refers to the Middle Way, the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*). As for the statement, "like the sound of a gong within a vessel resonating outward," this corresponds to the passage in this sutra concerning "the true emptiness of the nature of form" and so forth—how it is "pure and fundamental from the beginning, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. Now, I ask you in return:

when correlating such [teachings] regarding Perfect Enlightenment with the Three Kinds of Cessation (*tri-śamatha*) of Tiantai, is this a matter of forced interpretation or is it natural? How does it relate?
Is it not so? Is it consistent with [the principle of] engagement? Is it consistent, or is it inconsistent?

He further states: "Moreover, even that which the Tathāgata answered would entirely correspond to the three types of cessation (*śamatha*), and it too would fall within the errors identified by Tiantai.
For he explicitly stated that if *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are taken in isolation—like a single wheel or a solitary wing—they cannot [function]."
"To travel so far only to find that the questions and answers of the Buddha’s assemblies have instead emerged from beneath Tiantai—this is the height of absurdity.

Regarding the *Xuebang* (Dispelling Slander), it says: "To speak in such a manner is the height of confusing names and losing their true meaning. This is because worldly dharmas [and] supramundane..."

Regarding the relationship between names and phenomena: name and meaning are for the most part not congruent. The name is treated as the guest and the peripheral, while the meaning is treated as the host and the reality.
One must not allow a minor portion of the guest-name to undermine the majority of the host-meaning. Therefore, the Patriarch said:
"To seek meaning through names, one will find it not once in ten thousand cases; to determine names through meaning, one will fail not once in ten thousand cases. Thus spoke the Great Master.

Regarding the statement that those who possess "only a single wheel" or "but one wing" fall into the error of partial cultivation, this was said out of concern that beginners might become confused by the names and thereby lose sight of the meaning.

If we now explain the Great Samādhi by means of the three kinds of cessation (*tri-śamatha*), it is because we first establish the names according to their designations, and subsequently explain the names according to their meanings.
For instance, when Master Gushan explained it through the three cessations, he followed the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
*Śamatha*—this is translated as "calming" (*zhi*). *Vipaśyanā*—this is translated as "contemplation" (*guan*). *Upekṣā*—this is translated as "equanimity" (*zhiguan deng*).
Now, since the three names in this sutra share one point in common with the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* while differing on two points, they must derive three distinct meanings from within that *śamatha*:
namely, *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*. Master Yunjian’s critique of Gushan’s [interpretation]... [text ends].
The meaning of this explanation is most appropriate. To provide scriptural proof from the *Nirvana Sutra* (Yuánjué jīng), it says:

"For instance, regarding the three dharmas of the *Nirvana Sutra*, they are also referred to therein as 'samādhis. As it says: 'At that time, there were twenty-five kinds of pure wheels of samādhi,' and so forth.
Furthermore, it says: 'O Bianyin, you should know that the unimpeded, pure wisdom of all bodhisattvas all arises from...'"

It arises from meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), namely *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*. This indicates that even the Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*) may be explained directly as the three types of cessation (*tri-śamatha*);
how much more so the present sutra? For Ānanda, having already grown weary of mere erudition and limited wisdom, it was appropriate for him to request the Great Concentration (*mahā-samādhi*).
That it is now explained by means of the three cessations is because cessation belongs to the category of concentration. This...
Thus it is said that names are established based on names. However, if names are established based on their meaning, as the *Gushan Shu* (Commentary by Gushan) itself reconciles:
"These three types of cessation are themselves the three types of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), because they are quiescence while illuminating, and illumination while quiescent."
Therefore, *śamatha* is the contemplation of emptiness; *samādhi* is the contemplation of the provisional; and *dhyāna* is the contemplation of the Middle Way.
Thus, the *Huìjiě* (Comprehensive Explanation) states: "Now I shall further explain and clarify this: *śamatha* has the meaning of quiescence;

*samādhi* has the meaning of contemplative illumination; and *dhyāna* has the meaning of the non-duality of quiescence and illumination. This is likely derived from the synthesis of *zhǐguān* (calm abiding and insight) by Gushan.

This is merely the meaning of "penetration. Yet, Master Jiaoguang, desiring to greatly manifest the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and extensively refute various masters, ought to read each of the commentaries from antiquity in detail; he should preserve what is correct and reject what is erroneous.

Only when he had won over the hearts of the people did he become entirely indifferent; he concerned himself solely with his own rightness and others' wrongness, becoming so utterly deluded by names as to lose the underlying meaning.
To reach such a state of extreme self-entanglement, and then to claim that others are even more entangled—is this possible or impossible?
Second, there is the inconsistency of the structural analysis (*vibhāga*). To be confused about this is not merely to be confused about the scriptural text;

it leads to numerous internal contradictions even within one's own commentary. For example, although the old interpretations do not divide the text into minor sections, they do roughly divide it into three major sections:

first, the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*); second, the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*); and third, the Path of Realization (*sākṣāt-kriyā-mārga*). Since the first section is already called the "Path of Seeing," [the subsequent designations must likewise be consistent].
One should have already addressed the cultivation of the path (bhāvanāmārga), yet the cultivation of the path must depend on the subsequent section.

When it comes to explaining the text, one often searches for the three contemplations (trivipaśyanā) and assumes that this must be the cultivation of the path; however, in reality, the scriptural text originally contains no such thematic progression.
This is merely a forced interpretation outside of the text, for how could the literal reading possibly be teaching people to cultivate the three contemplations?
As for these words: even if one were to take one or two similar passages and force them into a harmonious interpretation, they would utterly lack any meaningful sense.

Recently, there have even been those who, while failing to refute the section on the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*), instead open up a large segment and arbitrarily assign it to the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*).

They fail to consider that "Path of Vision" refers to the realization of the principle of nature (*dharmatā*), whereas the "three contemplations" refer to the matter of progressive cultivation and effort.

Since it has already been stated that *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* constitute the cultivation of the Path (*mārga-bhāvanā*), why is it necessary to categorize them as belonging to the stage of the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*)?

Furthermore, if this stage were already the cultivation of the Path, then the Tathāgata would have merely instructed sentient beings to cultivate from the three contemplations until they reach the "perfect penetration" (*vibhūti-prativedha*) of the ear-faculty;
what, then, would be the purpose of [the subsequent stages]?
Xuemo said: "When I read to this point, I could not help but burst into laughter. I never imagined that this Master’s superficial views would reach such an extreme.
This matter requires no further debate; those with discernment can naturally distinguish between the fragrant and the putrid.

However, as there are many today within our realm who pursue what is foul-smelling, I have cleared this away for them, so as to avoid the fate of the white jade [being mistaken for dung] by the flies."

[The critic] defames [the text]. He cites the *Huìjiě* (Commentary on the Compendium) regarding the three sections, yet he fails to realize that the original work was actually divided into five major sections by Wēnlíng (*Yàojiě*:
Essential Commentary). These are: first, the Section on Seeing the Path; second, the Section on Cultivating the Path; third, the Section on Realizing the Fruit;

fourth, the Section on Concluding the Sūtra; and fifth, the Section on Aiding the Path. This is a judgment that remains unalterable for a thousand ages. For although Wēnlíng was a venerable scholar of the Chan school, he was in fact a master of the Teachings (*Jiào*).
Yuan Baiwei’s commentaries and exegeses demonstrate considerable skill; they are not merely the talk of a minor master who has studied mere words or those who prattle on about vague, "lumpen" Chan.

Regarding Gushan’s method of using the three types of cessation (*śamatha*) to explain the text, he also possesses his own topical outline (*ko*), yet Jiaoguang had not previously even glimpsed its boundaries.
Now, I shall first set forth the general outline of his judgments, harmonizing them with those of Wenling. However—
Subsequently, he directly refutes the errors of the *Zhengmai*. That work states that the major divisions of the "Section on the True Doctrine" (*zhèngzōngfēn*) consist of six parts:
first, relying on the eternally abiding true mind to open up the perfect understanding; this is identical to the "Section on Realizing the Way" (*jiàndàofēn*) in the *Wēnlíng* commentary.

Second, relying on the eternally abiding true mind to initiate perfect practice; this is identical to the "Section on Cultivating the Way" (*xiūdàofēn*). Third, relying on both the primary and auxiliary practices to distinguish the stages of perfection; this is...

1. The section on "Realizing the Fruit" (Zhengguo fen) is identical to [the corresponding part of the *Sūtra*]. 2. The fourth section, "Receiving and Upholding the Name" (Cheng ming shouchi), following the preparation of the three dharmas, is identical to the section on "Concluding the Sūtra" (Jie jing fen).
3. The fifth section, which extensively distinguishes the seven destinies (*sapta-gati*) while resolving remaining doubts, is identical to the "Aids to the Path" (Zhudao fen).

4. The sixth section, where the Buddha speaks spontaneously without being questioned to pre-clarify the meditative states (*dhyāna-viṣaya*), differs slightly from that [section]. This is because Wēn'gǎng combined the meditative states with the Aids to the Path, whereas here the Aids to the Path are opened up [as a separate section].

Such is the state of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Since the two masters have profoundly grasped the great purport in their judgments, how could their exegesis be confused regarding minor details?
It is simply that they first distinguish between the real and the false, and subsequently harmonize the real and the false, continuing thus until the fourth fascicle.
All of these merely serve to elucidate the principle of perfection (*yuanli*). Indeed, this principle of perfection is the very foundation of Great Samādhi.

How could it ever involve opening up a major section to rigidly assign the three contemplations (*sanguan*)? Even when there is a single instance of a meaning pertaining to the Two Vehicles, if one explains it by means of emptiness, provisionality, and the middle, this clarifies the Three Truths (*sandì*), not the Three Contemplations.
Various masters, unaware that the names for the truths and the contemplations are identical, have frequently made errors.
I am not at fault for misunderstanding this; nor is it surprising that Jiaoguang took the *satyas* (truths) as the objects of contemplation (*guan*).

It is a pity that Gushan merely saw that the scriptural text explains the principle as perfectly integrated (*yuanrong*) and possessing the meaning of the three *satyas*, yet lacked any textual passage regarding their sequential order.

Consequently, he interpreted them solely as being perfectly integrated, not daring to definitively judge which was true, which was false, and which was the Middle Way. He failed to realize that although the principle is perfectly integrated, [the text] does not lack the meaning of the three truths.
Yet, within the literary structure, there is a sequence that is clearly discernible despite its apparent lack of order.
For example, the passage from the *Awakening of Faith* cited above regarding the three dharmas elucidates the meaning of sequential progression as clearly as pointing at one's own palm.

However, the first three fascicles, which respond to Ānanda’s questions, clarify the sequence of the three truths by way of their non-sequential nature; whereas the fourth fascicle, responding to Pūrṇa’s inquiry, proceeds again by way of sequence.
This is specifically to clarify the three truths that are not sequential. As for the preceding sequential [explanation], Ānanda formulated it based on his own realization;

thus he said, "The Wondrously Profound, the Universal Retainer, the Immovable Honored One. Here, "Wondrously Profound" (miao-zhan) summarizes the True (zhen), "Universal Retainer" (zongchi) summarizes the Conventional (su), and "Immovable" (budong) summarizes the Middle (zhong).
As for the two non-sequential [explanations], the Tathāgata himself formulated them; thus he said, "And like..."
"The Tathāgatagarbha’s wondrously luminous primordial mind is neither mind nor empty," up to "constant, blissful, self, and pure"—this concludes the True Truth (paramārtha-satya).
"The Tathāgatagarbha’s primordial luminous mind is wondrous; it is precisely mind and precisely empty," etc.—this concludes the Conventional Truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
"The Tathāgatagarbha’s wondrously luminous primordial mind is free from 'is' and 'is not,' yet it is both 'is' and 'is not'"—this concludes the Middle Way. This is clearly explained and understood.
The meaning is as luminous as the bright sun adorning the sky; while people may criticize it, how could the Buddha be criticized?

As for the confused theories regarding the realization and cultivation of the Way, these have deviated from the authentic lineage and given rise to arbitrary interpretations, seeking out flaws with the utmost scrutiny.
First, there is something regarding this that remains unclear, which serves as the root of the entanglement; thus, the vines spread on and on without end.
Intending to use the axe-handle [to cut them], there have been further "guest" arguments—first, second, and third rescues—all of which are unworthy of being adopted.

Originally, I intended to set this aside without adjudication; however, it may also serve to clarify the correct principle. Therefore, I shall not avoid prolixity and will briefly provide an analysis.

Zhengmei establishes three points for the guest’s defense. First, he states that there is a distinction in the Wu-xing edition between "general invitation" (*tong-qing*) and "specific invitation" (*bie-qing*).

He suggests that the preceding three contemplations likely correspond to the general invitation, while the cultivation of the profound mind and its return to perfect penetration correspond to the specific invitation.
[Question: Such is the skillful means for the beginner. [Answer: If this is indeed so, then these should both be included in the preceding section on the "Path of Cultivation" (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
Yet, within that Path of Cultivation, they are further divided into two sections: first, the cultivation of the general invocation; second, the cultivation of the specific invocation.

Only in this way is that explanation established. Why is it that, although both share the meaning of "cultivation," one section is designated as the "Path of Vision" (*darśana-mārga*) and the other as the "Path of Cultivation"?

Is this so? Furthermore, since the two practices of the shallow and the deep have already been distinguished, a beginner must first practice *yuantong* (perfect penetration) and subsequently practice the three contemplations (*sanguan*).
I venture to ask: to what stage or rank does one who practices *yuantong* reach before it becomes a "deep mind," at which point one may then practice the three contemplations?
Now, according to the Bodhisattva’s own account, from the initial entry into the stream up until the manifestation of quiescence (*jimiexianqian*), [it is clear that...]

Without yet attaining the state of uninterrupted cultivation of the three contemplations, the Tathāgata nevertheless says that this faculty is "initially liberated," having first attained the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

According to the stages, this corresponds to the seventh stage of faith (*śraddhā*), which is equal to a *śrāvaka* Arhat. Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva reaches the point where "that which is heard and the hearing itself are exhausted," he seems to correspond to this stage.

It is further stated that when "the nature of emptiness is perfectly luminous," one achieves the liberation of phenomena (*dharma-vimokṣa*). According to the stages, this corresponds to the eighth or ninth stage of faith. Thus it has been said.

Surpassing the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) of the Hīnayāna, the emptiness of the emptiness of the Bodhisattva seems to correspond to this stage. Furthermore, it says that once the dharmas of liberation have been understood, both [subject and object] are empty and do not arise.

According to the stages, this should correspond to the fulfillment of the tenth mind of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā-citta*), which is subsequently judged to be the stage of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
To abide in this position is precisely what was meant by "abiding in the original dwelling. Yet, when the Bodhisattva’s quiescence manifests before them, it is precisely at this very stage.
Is this not, then, already the stage of the profound mind (*gambhīra-citta*)? Why is there no mention of connecting with the cultivation of the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) here?

Could it be that one only begins to cultivate them in a subsequent stage? Nevertheless, at this stage, the Bodhisattva has already transcended both the mundane and supramundane realms, giving rise to the three categories of boundless [virtues].
As for these sublime functions, could it be that the three contemplations taught by Tiantai are not even capable of being cultivated by Bodhisattvas of the stage of Equal Enlightenment?
And are all those who practice the three contemplations today Bodhisattvas of the first abode or above? Such a view is profoundly mistaken.
Xue Bang said: "Wuxing Yuan previously made a judgment regarding 'general' and 'specific' invitations.
He stated that the three dharmas of *śamatha* are called 'general' because they were collectively cultivated by all Tathāgatas throughout the ten directions;

the faculty of the ear is called 'specific' because it is the particular means for the practitioner in this land to trigger and practice them. The reason Ānanda requested both the general and the specific was..."

If the general were not distinct from the particular, then the general would have no gateway through which to enter. If the particular were not permeated by the general, then the particular would become a mere practice of phenomenal forms.
Just as among worldly people, who is without the six sense organs? Yet, to establish cognition based on seeing and knowing is the very root of ignorance.
How could the Buddhas be without the six sense organs? To have no seeing within seeing and knowing—this is precisely Nirvana. As the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "It is like a person who..."

The eyes are illuminated by the light of the sun, whereby various forms are seen; this is what is meant. If the text is divided according to two gates, then the first four fascicles constitute the Section on the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*).
This responds to the general request [to enter the palace], as in the phrase "please enter the flowered hall. It also responds to the specific request.
The general answer is that it merely causes one to see the Path; the specific answer is that it causes one to cultivate the Path. As Master Wenling said:
"First one sees the Path, and thereafter one cultivates the Path; first one cultivates the Path, and thereafter one realizes the Fruit. This is the standard sequence.
However, if a swift horse, upon seeing the shadow of a whip, immediately enters the correct road, why be bound by the standard sequence? As for Ānanda, having heard of the Path...
Thereafter, one does not pass through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* but immediately attains the Dharmakāya; how could this be constrained by ordinary conventions?
However, to serve as an eye for future generations, I cannot help but make this determination. This principle is also extremely simple and accessible;
even a minor disciple who merely studies the words can understand it for himself. Why then must one laboriously set forth questions and answers to refute others?
This is precisely what is called "discussing the great Peng bird by means of a vinegar gnat.

Since this has already been understood, there is no need to labor over the arguments regarding the claim that one must first practice *yuan-tong* (perfect penetration) and only later practice the three contemplations (*san-guan*).

Nevertheless, it is also an essential matter to clarify the relative depths of the three contemplations and the characteristics of their cultivation based on this, so as to instruct others in this knowledge. Therefore, I shall instruct you as follows:
There are three contemplations for those at the initial stage and three contemplations for those at the profound stage.

The three contemplations for the initial stage refer to practitioners of the present who must, from the very moment they set out on the path, maintain a moment-to-moment illumination of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.

The three contemplations for the profound stage refer to what is explained in the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (Yingluo jing) regarding the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) of Bodhisattvas, wherein the three contemplations only manifest upon reaching those stages. The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* also speaks in this same manner.

It is so. If this sutra is compared with the three types of cessation-and-contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) cultivated in the *Complete Enlightenment* (*Yuánjué*), it encompasses both the beginning and the end, as well as the shallow and the deep.
For instance, within the stage of Dry Wisdom (*gāndhī-bhūmi*), one enters the flow of the center within the center by means of this very mind;

reaching the first abode (*prathama-bhūmi*), one proceeds from there with true skillful means, giving rise to these ten minds, continuing all the way up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Because this is the cultivation of cessation-and-contemplation, the *Adornment Sutra* (*Yíngluò jīng*) states: "Equal Enlightenment..."

"Shining-Quiescence" (*zhào-jì*) and "Wondrous Enlightenment—Quiescent-Shining" (*miào-jué-jì-zhào*) are both alternative names for the single essence of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight).

If explained in this way, then when a beginner practices perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*), they are practicing the three contemplations (*sān-guān*). How so? At the moment of entering the stream, one clearly perceives that the nature of hearing is profoundly still and pure;
this is the contemplation of emptiness (*kōng-guān*), which is the *śamatha* of realizing the reality of the body. One clearly perceives the hearing...
The essence of nature is the Dharma-realm; its ability to universally sustain all phenomena is the provisional contemplation (*parikalpita-śamatha*).
To clearly illuminate that the nature of hearing is eternally concentrated and immovable is the middle contemplation (*paratantra-dhyāna*), which is the cessation of the two extremes (*anta-dvaya*).

What was previously called the "Wondrously Profound Universal Sustainer, the Immovable Honored One" refers to this very point as the method for progressive cultivation; the meaning must reach this before it is complete. Now, regarding Avalokiteśvara...
Regarding the sequence of practices described, although the text consists of four sections, the principle must necessarily be revealed instantaneously.

As it is said—“the external objects vanish, the internal faculties are exhausted, the wisdom of emptiness is realized, and the principle of the Truth of Cessation is attained,” culminating in the manifestation of quiescent extinction—it is essential that these be fully perfected within a single thought-moment.

This corresponds to the names of the fruit-stage (phala-avasthā). If one were to forcibly assign these to the stages (bhūmi) and interpret them as shallow or deep according to the literal words, it would be like "hammering in a stake while rocking the oars.
How is this different from taking a mind of birth-and-death as the fundamental cause of cultivation, in order to seek the fruit of non-arising and non-ceasing?
As for what the Sūtra says: "Suddenly transcending the mundane and supramundane... [self...]

There are ordinary people who attain sudden enlightenment; such as the butcher Guang'e, who, upon laying down his butcher's knife, was immediately included among the number of the thousand Buddhas of the future.
Thus, one must not restrict them by means of ordinary sentiments.

As for the "two rescues" and "three rescues" of the Guest in the text, there is no distinction made between explaining principle and explaining practice, nor is there any distinction made between teaching awakening and teaching cultivation. This is quite a waste of effort.
There are many who possess numerous lips and tongues; yet all of them fail to understand that [delusion] arises from a lack of clarity regarding the Path of Seeing and the Path of Cultivation.

From delusion they accumulate further delusion, their confusion never ceasing. Since this has already been clearly explained above, the roots of this tangle have been severed; it is to be hoped that future students will not allow them to spread further.
As for the doctrine of the "fixed nature" (prakṛti-sthiti), this is a point well-discussed by Tiantai, yet you have rashly and erroneously rejected it.
To take the nature of delusion as the very basis for *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*—how easy is this to discuss! Now I ask: Has Jiaoguang ever thoroughly practiced the Tiantai *śamatha-vipaśyanā*?

Has he ever read to mastery the Tiantai *Yuan-dun zhi-guan* (Perfect and Sudden Śamatha-Vipaśyanā), the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra), the *Wenju* (Textual Commentary), and other such works?
When one examines his [interpretation] of the principle that "the entirety of nature gives rise to cultivation" and "the entirety of cultivation resides within nature," it is completely...
I understand. Or perhaps you have mistakenly taken the *satyas* (truths) for the *vipaśyanā* (insight) and the *vipaśyanā* for the *satyas*.
If so, you have not mastered the meaning of the *satyas* and *vipaśyanā*; it is only natural that you have neither practiced them nor studied them thoroughly.
This point ought to be discussed with him in detail, but as there is further text below, I shall set it aside for now.

Furthermore, it is said: If one were to cultivate the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) directly within the state of perfect penetration, then since the nature of hearing fundamentally takes its essence in non-discrimination, one would simply reverse the hearing and enter directly with a single blade.
Thus, at the outset, the six consciousnesses are discarded, and neither investigation (*vitarka*), analysis (*vicāra*), nor discursive thought (*manasikāra*) is employed.
As the verse says: "Investigation and analysis arise from discursive thought; body and mind cannot reach them. Now, if one were to add the three contemplations to this, then—

If one continues to engage in discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*), how could one ever transcend the six consciousnesses? Thus, it would be incorrect for the Tathāgata to prioritize the destruction of the six consciousnesses at the outset.

If they were to be cultivated after [the realization of] perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa-vidyā*), then one should understand that such an error was already addressed in the analysis of the various stages of depth and shallowness [in the preceding chapters].
Since these three periods are all rendered useless in this way, how can you falsely attribute to the Buddha’s intention a position identical to yours?

Is this not the Three Contemplations of Tiantai? Furthermore, since that wise minister truly understands the King’s intent—being neither mistaken nor erroneous—the King should have no need to further alter his decree.
Thus, when the Buddha later requested that [the practice] be cultivated, he should have merely pointed to the Three Contemplations mentioned in the preceding text for cultivation.
Why then did he separately speak of "hearing by turning back" as the method of cultivation? Since he has now spoken of it separately, it cannot be disregarded.

The three contemplations (samādhis) sufficiently prove that what was previously presented was merely the disclosure of the principle-body of inherent nature (*xingju liti*), which does not inherently contain the three contemplations.
How could these various masters truly be ministers with the wisdom of a Universal Monarch?
Xuebang said: "When I first read the *Zhengmo*, I observed how it could so eloquently expound upon the nature of seeing (jianxing) as taught by the Tathāgata;
I marveled at it with the utmost admiration. Now, however, observing this current discourse, it seems they only know that nature but do not know its concentration (ding).

As for the complete cultivation of the ear-door, it is much like trying to catch the wind or grasp a shadow. It may be called the 'path of seeing' (jendao), but if one speaks of the 'path of cultivation' (xiudao), I—"
I did not yet dare to grant permission. Why? It is because the Dharma-gate of Perfect Penetration possesses both the aspect of nature (*xing*) and the aspect of cultivation (*xiu*).

As seen in Mañjuśrī’s selection, he spoke mostly of nature and little of cultivation; whereas in Avalokiteśvara’s exposition, he spoke mostly of cultivation and little of nature. Thus, the verse says:
"When drums are struck simultaneously in the ten directions, they are heard at once in all ten locations. This is the perfect reality, hearing sounds through a wall."
An echo can be heard both far and near; this is the universal reality. Sound is neither non-existent nor extinguished; sound is neither existent nor born.

Being perfectly free from both birth and extinction—this is the eternal reality. This reveals that the nature of Avalokiteśvara and the nature of sentient beings are identical in the ear, and nowhere is it otherwise.
It continues: "Even if one is in a dream, it does not cease because of the lack of thought."
There is none. When it is said that "discernment and investigation transcend thought, such that body and mind cannot reach them," this refers to the state within dreams.
For example, as previously mentioned, one might be confused enough to mistake a pestle for a bell or drum, yet still find it strange when it produces the sound of wood or stone.

Such discernment and investigation within a dream—vivid and lucid—is independent of thought; it emerges beyond the realm of thought. This, then, simply means that the nature of hearing does not depend on [deliberate] thought.

Contemplate this: when has it ever been said that there is no vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought) altogether? If one were to say they are entirely absent, how would this differ from wood or stone?

One must know that this "emergence" spoken of here is an emergence that transcends; it is not an emergence that comes forth from within the realm of discursive thought. If it were an emergence produced from such thought, [it would not be true emergence].
This would be a misunderstanding of the meaning of the text. One must understand that these words concern *xing* (nature), not yet *xiu* (cultivation).
If one considers the four stages of practice described by Avalokiteśvara—“entering the stream and losing the object”—these speak mostly of cultivation and little of nature.
