This is not so. How can this be reconciled?
This is the fourth question. Some attempt to reconcile it by saying: "Since it is said that [the teaching] 'selects' the sages, it depends entirely upon selecting the capacities [of the listeners].

If the Tathāgata [addresses] Mañjuśrī, it is because he wishes to bring about the simultaneous awakening of the capacities of sentient beings; what harm is there in his own capacity also being included among those selected?"
Regarding the wondrous nature of seeing one's nature: how could this be any different for the sages?

If it is so—that seeing one's nature is granted as wondrous in the case of the sages—then may it not likewise be granted that the nature of smelling, the nature of tasting, the nature of sensation, and the nature of cognition are all gates of awakening for the sages, and are thus equally wondrous?

The fifth question: Following the scripture’s clarification of the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*), it subsequently reconciles all phenomena, stating that the eighteen realms (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*) and the seven elements (*sapta-mahābhūta*) are all fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous true *tathatā*-nature.
Since the five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya*) are already admitted to be wondrous in the state of a sage, is it not likewise admitted that the dharmas are also wondrous?
The sixth question: The insentience of the six objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) is certainly beyond dispute; however, may it also be granted that the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*) are likewise wondrous?
The seventh question: Is the wondrousness of the six faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) identical to the sentient beings' six faculties of experience (*upabhoga-indriya*), or is it distinct from them?
If it were distinct, then sentient beings would possess no wondrousness to manifest, and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* should not have said: "Desiring to cause..."
Sentient beings open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. If they are identical [to the Buddha], why are sentient beings not called Buddhas?
If they are neither identical nor separate, please explain this clearly.
The eighth question: The six consciousnesses may likewise be identical to the six sense organs. Does this clarify that they are neither identical nor separate?

If they are not identical, how can it be said within the eighteen *dhātus* that they are fundamentally the *tathāgatagarbha*? If they are not separate, why did the World-Honored One first refute the six consciousnesses?

The Ninth Question: Since the Tathāgata first refuted the six consciousnesses and later elucidated the *tathāgatagarbha* in the text, why does he only reveal the subtlety of the six consciousnesses, while never once mentioning the eighth or ninth consciousness? As the "Great Text on Consciousness" (*Shi-da-wen*) states:
Within this consciousness, you shall successively point them out: "This is Mañjuśrī," "This is Pūrṇa," and so forth.
Then, after conducting a thorough investigation through the four propositions, he reveals the wondrous truth, saying:

"If this conscious mind originally has no source from which it arises, yet is capable of knowing, discerning, seeing, hearing, perceiving, and cognizing—perfectly full and profoundly still—its nature does not originate from any external locus. (And so on. Since [he] first...
□ It is not appropriate to [discuss] "immediacy" (ji). Later immediacy. The beginning should not be broken.
What is the ultimate purport? The tenth question: Within the section on manifesting the merits of the mind-faculty (manas-indriya), it says:

"Like the silent receptivity of the mind, it encompasses all worldly and world-transcending dharmas throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time—whether saintly or ordinary—without exception, reaching to their very limits. When...
One knows the faculty of mind (*manas*). It is fully endowed with one thousand two hundred merits. Is this faculty of mind identical to or different from the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)?
As the Sūtra says: "If it were identical to the mind, how could there be that which is produced? If it were different from the mind, they would not be the same, and there would be no cognition.
If there were no cognition, how could the mind arise? If there is cognition, how can one cognize the mind?"
Since both identity and difference lack established nature, how can the elements (*dhātu*) be established? Thus, both identity and difference are untenable.

The conclusion at the end states: "If these three locations are entirely non-existent, then mind, dharmas, and the mind-element—these three—are fundamentally neither conditioned by causes and conditions nor of a spontaneous nature.
If, in total, these three locations are entirely non-existent, then the subsequent manifestation of merit is solely...
What is it that is called "encompassing all without exception, both the holy and the ordinary"? If one says it is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor spontaneous,
yet is eternally abiding, wondrously luminous, immovable, and all-pervading— the wondrous nature of True Suchness (tathatā) which becomes even more manifest because of this—
what does this meaning signify?
The eleventh question: The Tiantai school clarifies that a single moment of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) possesses the ten dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*).

Is this identical to, or different from, the meaning of the faculty of mind (*manas*) in this sutra, which silently accommodates all mundane and supramundane phenomena throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, encompassing both the sacred and the profane without exception?

The Twelfth Question: Relying on this sūtra to cultivate the dharma-gate of the ear-faculty, regarding the four types of samādhi, does one practice by long sitting, by long walking, by half-walking and half-sitting, or by neither walking nor sitting?
The thirteenth question: If one is walking, there is movement rather than stillness, and the nature of hearing is difficult to manifest. Therefore, the text states:
"For example, when a person dwells in stillness"—it is clear that this means it is appropriate to sit and not appropriate to walk.
The fourteenth question: If one practices long-term sitting meditation, does one keep the eyes open or closed?
If the eyes are kept open, how does this differ from ordinary seeing? If the eyes are kept closed, how does this differ from contemplating the mind?
The fifteenth question: If one opens their eyes, is it also permitted to hear and see? Or is it also permitted to see and hear?
If one closes their eyes, is it also permitted for the mind to hear? Or is it also permitted for the mind to hear?
The sixteenth question: The Sūtra clarifies that when one sees the seeing, it is necessarily unmoving and necessarily without transition, extending even to being necessarily vast and pure.
These qualities all manifest when one opens the eyes and observes objects, such that everything before the eyes is transparently clear.

But as for when one closes the eyes and observes internally—whether in darkness without a lamp or when the appearance of obscurity manifests before one—how does one see that seeing? And as for [the state] compared to that...
Is it the meaning of "greatness" and so forth?
This is the seventeenth question. At the beginning of the Sūtra’s revelation of the nature of seeing, it uses the analogy of a blind person staring into darkness; this is the mind and not the eye.
When one opens the eyes and sees light, sees forms, sees space, and so on, is this also the mind and not the eye?
The eighteenth question: When a blind person gazes into darkness, is this mind not the mind of the eyes? Is it the eternally abiding true mind, or not?
If it is not, then it would be identical to these ten meanings discussed below.
If it is, why is it that at the time of gazing into darkness, these ten meanings do not manifest?
The nineteenth question: Within the context of the aggregates (*skandha*) and their objects, it is said that non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) previously revered and served water and fire.
Now, "revering" means to honor, and "serving" means to attend upon. To honor the Way and serve the Buddha—these are indeed acts of service; they are fundamentally the same as serving water and fire.

For what reason do the practices of the non-Buddhists lead to heterodoxy? [In contrast,] Ucchuṣma and the youth Candraprabha revere and serve [the Buddha], yet [they do not fall into error]. Why is this so?
Is it through the realization of the Way?

This is the twentieth question. Now, the mind of consciousness is indeed one and the same. For what reason do the Buddhas and Patriarchs clarify it so that one may achieve Great Enlightenment, while Kāśyapa extinguishes it so that one may realize the Four Fruits [of the Śrāvaka], and ordinary people cultivate it so that they become non-Buddhists?
The twenty-first question: The sutra text refutes the deluded mind as having no location. Letan said: "This refutation of the delusion is intended to cause one to recognize the original truth.
He cited an ancient master, saying: "Seeking the mind throughout the three periods of time, the mind is not found; where the mind is not found, delusion is fundamentally non-existent.
Where deluded mind is non-existent is Bodhi; birth-and-death and Nirvana are fundamentally equal. (Gu) [End]
Mount Yun said: "One should know that the Tathāgata pursued and shattered [delusion] at seven points, leaving this infinitesimal deluded mind with no place to flee.
Once the bandit of delusion is eliminated, the True King is revealed; herein the principle of non-arising is seen.
Is such an interpretation appropriate or not? Does it perceive the Way or not?"

The twenty-second question: In the "Chapter on the Universal Eye of Perfect Enlightenment," prior to the elucidation of *śamatha*, one is first instructed to examine the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) to investigate the body, thereby realizing that the body has no marks of a body;
next, one is instructed to scrutinize the mind by means of the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), thereby realizing that the mind has no marks of a mind.
Is this the same as, or different from, the refutation of delusion found in this sutra?
The twenty-third question: The Second Patriarch of the Chan school asked the First Patriarch, "My mind is not at peace; I beg the Master to grant me peace of mind.
The First Patriarch said, "Bring forth your mind, and I shall pacify it for you. The Second Patriarch replied, "When I search for my mind, it is utterly unobtainable.

The Patriarch said, "I have finished pacifying your mind. This is consistent with the investigation of the mind and the refutation of the self in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra*.
"Is the mind the same as [the object] or different?
This is the twenty-fourth question. Regarding the Tiantai *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*, one investigates the nature of the mind through four propositions:
Is the mind so called because it is caused by the mind? Or is it so called because it is not caused by the mind? Or is it so called because it is both caused by the mind and not caused by the mind?"
Is the mind neither caused by the mind nor uncaused by the mind? Is this the same as, or different from, the two sutras of the Chan school?
This is the twenty-fifth question. Between the *Yuanjue jing* (Complete Enlightenment Sutra) and the *Lengyan jing* (Śūraṅgama Sūtra), which is superior and which inferior?

The twenty-sixth question: In the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the clarity of the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*) is emphasized as being most intimate; in the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā*), the meaning of awakened awareness (*bodhi*) is taken as paramount.

If one speaks in terms of the nature of seeing, then the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* should yield its ground; if one speaks in terms of the meaning of awakening, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* ought to take a step back.
Is this possible, or is it not?

The twenty-seventh question: The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* is extensive in its text yet subtle in its meaning; the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna* is concise in its text yet comprehensive in its principle.
Is it appropriate to study the *Śūraṅgama* first and then the *Awakening of Faith*, or is it not?

The twenty-eighth question: The *Awakening of Faith in Mahāyāna* (Yuanjue) is for the capacity of Bodhisattvas; it is perfect and sudden. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* (Lengyan) is for the capacity of Śrāvakas;
it is perfect and gradual. Is it appropriate to rank the *Awakening of Faith* as the elder and the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* as the younger? Or is this not permissible?

The twenty-ninth question: In the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (Yuánjué jīng), cultivation is long while the nature is short; in the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra* (Léngyán jīng), cultivation is short while the nature is long.
Is it permissible for these two to defer to one another, or is it not?

Question Thirty: Regarding the luminous awakening of *pariniṣpanna-bodhi* (perfectly realized enlightenment), is there a separate, great awakening apart from the awakened mind of the six consciousnesses of sentient beings?

Or is it simply the very awareness of sentient beings? If it were the latter, why would the *Jianzhang* not state that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions possess a great *dhāraṇī* called "Perfect Awakening" (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*), which gives rise to all pure [phenomena]?

Regarding pure *tathatā*: if one were to separate them, it would contradict what follows below, which states: "To know illusion is itself to leave it; no expedient means need be employed. To leave illusion is itself awakening;

there is no gradual progression. Furthermore, it says: "When a Tathāgata cultivates Perfect Awakening during the causal stage, he knows these are like flowers in the sky, and thus there is no cyclic existence.
Between "knowing" (*ji*) and "leaving" (*li*), please choose the correct interpretation.

The thirty-first question: Although the characteristics of dharmas are manifold, they take the single mind as their foundation. Although the gateways of practice are immeasurable, they take the meaning of awakening as their core principle.
Is it permissible for the *Complete Enlightenment* and the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* to alternate as guest and host? Or is it not?
The thirty-second question: Ānanda originally requested the sublime *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*.
Regarding the "perfect penetration of the ear-faculty," one should practice by adopting the meaning of the preceding [explanation]. This is like the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*:

taking stillness as the practice for *śamatha*, taking illusory transformation as the practice for *samādhi*, and taking non-grasping as the practice for *dhyāna*. As Jiaoguang has said, the ear-faculty fundamentally takes its essence as its basis.
Non-discrimination. To enter directly with a single blade—does this encompass the whole leopard, or only a single spot?
This is the thirty-third question. If the essence of fruition is indeed non-discriminatory, then the task would be complete;
how then should one understand the sequence of practices described in the subsequent text, such as "gradually increasing" and so forth?

Question thirty-four: In the "Explanation of Terms" (*Shiming*) within the *Tiantai Zhiguan*, there are "stopping-and-staying cessation" (*tingzhi zhi*), "stopping-to-rest cessation" (*zhixi zhi*), and "stopping-by-stopping cessation" (*zhizhi zhi*).

There are also "penetrating contemplation" (*guanchuan guan*), "thorough-reaching contemplation" (*guanda guan*), and "non-contemplation contemplation" (*buguan guan*). These are all conventional distinctions;

they do not pertain to the Perfect and Sudden [Teaching]. If one simply realizes that the essence is non-discriminatory, one does not lean toward the "stopping-and-staying" of stopping-and-staying cessation, nor toward the fixing of the mind.
Is this not the principle?

This is the thirty-fifth question. As discussed in the *Susang* (Suspended Discourse), the three cessations (*tri-śamatha*) are not permitted; since their essence is non-discriminative, how could they be merely one-sided aspects of the three?
The thirty-sixth question: If the fruit does not employ *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, why does Mañjuśrī speak of them again?

[The Master] replied: "When purity reaches its ultimate limit, light penetrates through; stillness and illumination encompass empty space. Is this not the meaning of *śamatha* as you call it—the sense of quiescence;
the meaning of *samādhi*—the sense of contemplative observation; and the meaning of *dhyāna*—the non-duality of stillness and illumination?
The thirty-seventh question: The Tathāgata asked Purna, "Fundamental enlightenment is wondrously luminous; the nature of enlightenment is luminously wondrous.

Is this luminosity not the illumination that is identical with stillness? Is this wondrousness not the stillness that is identical with illumination? Since the nature is fundamentally both still and illuminating, is it not through cessation and contemplation that one can restore it?"
The thirty-eighth question: A verse by Mañjuśrī states: "The nature of the ocean of awakening is limpid and perfect; this perfect limpidity of awakening is fundamentally subtle and wondrous.

Fundamental luminosity shines forth, giving rise to objects; this clearly indicates that the nature is inherently still and illuminating. Sentient beings, because of their illumination, forget their stillness, and thus there is birth and death.
Is it not through *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* that one can return to the source?"
The thirty-ninth question: The Tathāgata clarified the root of the illnesses of sentient beings, saying:
"To take a state of confused agitation as the nature of the mind—this single delusion constitutes the mind, and one becomes decisively deluded, regarding it as being within the physical body.

To be thus mired in ignorance is to obscure *prajñā*; can this be destroyed without contemplation? To be agitated and deluded is to obstruct liberation; can this be destroyed without tranquility? To be deluded within the physical body..."
The Dharma-body: can it not be realized through the non-duality of cessation and contemplation?
Question Forty: The Sūtra clarifies the beginning of delusion in four places. First, it says: "Obscured darkness becomes space"—is this not confusion?
Next, it says: "Delusion becomes luminous awareness; because of luminosity, an object is established"—is this not movement? Third, it says: "Luminous awareness is obscured..."
Obscurity and clarity depend upon one another to produce agitation. Is it not the case that when the characteristics of darkness and movement combine, they lead to great agitation?

The fourth [verse] says: "The primordial luminosity shines forth, giving rise to the objective realm; is this not movement? This, then, is the fundamental nature. Fundamentally, luminosity is stillness; delusion begins from this fundamental state.
When one returns to the origin, it is fundamentally dark and agitated. Can this be achieved without the practice of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight)?
The forty-first question: Do the twenty-five sages each describe a gateway to the ultimate realization, or do they describe the inner sanctum itself?
The forty-second question: If these are gateways, are they the gateway to a single hall, or are they the gateways to each individual hall?
Question Forty-three: Regarding the "innermost sanctum" to which one returns—does this refer to the innermost sanctum of a single hall, or the innermost sanctums of each individual hall?
Question Forty-four: If it refers to the innermost sanctums of each individual hall, then Mañjuśrī should not have said, "The nature of returning to the source is non-dual."
Question forty-five: In the innermost chamber of a single hall, is there a distinction between those who enter deeply and those who enter shallowly, or is there no such distinction?

Question forty-six: If there is indeed a distinction between entering deeply and shallowly, then the judgment made by Wu Xing regarding "complete entry" and "partial entry"—is this appropriate or not?
The forty-seventh question: If it is admitted that there is both a whole and a half, is the profound emptiness perceived [in each] the same or different?
The forty-eighth question: Is the vision that perceives profound emptiness distant or immediate?

Question forty-nine: Regarding the inner sanctum that is seen, is it merely empty? Is there something therein? Is there distinction between noble and base? Or is there no such distinction between noble and base? Question fifty:
As for the people within the hall and chamber, can those outside simultaneously see what is inside? Can those inside simultaneously see what is outside?
The fifty-first question: If it is granted that [Avalokiteśvara] hears and sees, would it be permissible for Avalokiteśvara to change names to Aniruddha?

Or would it not be permissible? The fifty-second question: If it is granted that [Aniruddha] sees and hears, would it be permissible for Aniruddha to change names to Avalokiteśvara? Or would it not be permissible?
The fifty-third question: If it is granted that the mind hears, is it permissible to change the name of Avalokiteśvara to Samantabhadra?
Or is it not? The fifty-fourth question: If it is granted that the mind hears, is it permissible to change the name of Samantabhadra to Avalokiteśvara? Or is it not?
Question fifty-five: When a Bodhisattva is called Avalokiteśvara, does this refer to observing with the eyes or observing with the mind?

Question fifty-six: If it is as the Wēnlíng commentary explains—that one observes it with the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) and not hears it with the auditory consciousness—then if that were entirely the case, how could a Bodhisattva alone be able to observe its sound with the mind, yet be unable to [hear it]?
Regarding the phrase "its sound":
this is the fifty-seventh question. Since the Bodhisattva is titled Avalokiteśvara (Guanyin), he not only hears what is heard, but also hears the sound—that is, the voice.
Kātyāyana heard the voice and entered the Path; thus, Avalokiteśvara is named after Kātyāyana.
Is it permissible or not permissible for Dignāga to become Avalokiteśvara?

This is the fifty-eighth question. Since the samādhi of the gateway of the ear has already been perfected as universal penetration, is it permissible or not permissible for one to hear hearing, smell smelling, taste tasting, feel feeling, and know knowing?
The fifty-ninth question: It is heard that the nature of hearing (*śrotra-dhātu*) is endowed with the three qualities of being perfect (*paripūrṇa*), universal (*samanta*), and constant (*nitya*).

Yet, when distinguishing it from the nature of seeing (*cakṣur-dhātu*), it is said only that "in the four intermediate directions, one half is deficient. This implies it lacks only a small portion of perfection.
How could this allow Nanda the Elder to directly rank above the stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*) of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva? Is this possible or not?

Question Sixty: When opening the eyes, one sees light; yet when observing the nature of seeing, although it may be partially impaired, if one closes the eyes and sees darkness, and observes the nature of seeing therein, it has no spatial location.
Is it possible for Nalakūvara to be of the same rank as Avalokiteśvara, or is it not?

The sixty-first question: If the olfactory faculty does not apprehend the act of smelling fragrance, but one contemplates only its inherent nature of being able to smell, would it also possess the meaning of being perfect, pervasive, and constant?
Would this allow one to join the ranks of those who contemplate Avalokiteśvara? Is this possible or not?
Question Sixty-Two: When the faculty of the tongue does not grasp at tastes, but merely observes the tranquil nature of awareness, is its perfect penetration complete or not?
The sixty-third question: The faculty of the body perceives only that which is capable of being sensed. This sensation is fundamentally without limit or measure.
Is it eternal? Or is it incomplete?

Question Sixty-four: When the faculty of mind does not grasp at or differentiate mental objects (*dharmas*), and all conditions are set aside so that [the mind] stands firm—does it possess the qualities of perfection, completeness, constancy, and universality? Or does it not?

The sixty-fifth question: Regarding the sensory object of form, one does not form conceptual attachments toward it, but simply contemplates that the nature of form is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true form—pure and fundamental from the outset, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. Is this perfect penetration, or is it not?

The sixty-sixth question: Regarding the sense-object of sound, one does not grasp at the words and speech of the Dharma, but rather grasps the silence within all sounds to manifest my own spiritual nature.
Is this complete penetration? Or is it not complete penetration?
Question Sixty-Seven: Lingyun attained enlightenment upon seeing peach blossoms, and Kāśyapa broke into a smile upon seeing the udumbara flower.
Is the realm of form perfectly penetrating? Or is it not perfectly penetrating?
Question Sixty-Eight: Xiangyan struck a bamboo to clarify the mind, and Guanyin heard sounds to restore his nature.
Is the auditory object (śabda-viṣaya) perfectly penetrating? Or is it not perfectly penetrating?
Question Sixty-Nine: The two vehicles originally enter the Path by hearing sounds, and are thus called Śrāvakas (Hearers).
Is it now appropriate to call Xiangyan a Śrāvaka? Or is it not?
The seventieth question: Avalokiteśvara is both the observer and the observed, yet he has awakened to the Way. Is it permissible to refer to Avalokiteśvara as a *śrāvaka*?
Or is it not? The seventy-first question: To seek through movement is to attain knowledge by means of the union of fragrance and sincerity. To observe through stillness—[is this not the same?]
The nature of smelling is constantly perceived; is it universally pervasive, or is it not?
This is the seventy-second question. When sweet and bitter flavors do not reach the tongue-root, there is nevertheless a natural, bland taste;
its perception is always uniform—is this universally pervasive, or is it not?
Seventy-third question: A person possesses a body that never ceases to be subject to contact;
indeed, it does not wait for the coming together [of conditions] to be perceived, being ever thus. Is this universally pervasive, or is it not?

The seventy-fourth question: The dharma-object (dharmāyatana) is the shadow left behind by the falling away of the five objects. If even the five objects are themselves empty, how much more so is the dharma-object?
When one realizes that the source of dharmas is fundamentally non-existent and that there is neither subject nor object, is this not perfect penetration?
Is it not perfect penetration?
The seventy-fifth question: What is the distance between the faculty of sight and the consciousness of sight? When perceiving form, do their essences not differ?
Are they universally pervasive, or are they not?

The seventy-sixth question: The mind-hearing of Samantabhadra penetrates the ten directions. At the stage of fruition, it is "Great Penetration," whereas at the causal stage, it is "Small Penetration.
Since even the faculty of hearing is said to increase gradually, does this not conflict with the initial mind? Is it complete in its essence yet minute in its manifestation?
Is it perfectly penetrating, or is it not?
Question seventy-seven: The nose does not grasp its perceptions, but grasps only its sensations. Is this complete penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*)? Or is it incomplete? Question seventy-eight:
The tongue plays with sounds and characters; setting aside those that have spatial divisions capable of signifying [meaning], it grasps only...
That which is expounded is a principle that is inexhaustible and likewise possesses one thousand two hundred merits. Is it perfectly penetrating? Or is it not perfectly penetrating?
This is the seventy-ninth question: bodily consciousness is not necessarily restricted to the observance or violation of precepts; rather, one simply takes that which is constantly aware.
Is it perfect penetration? Is it not perfect penetration?

The eightieth question: If consciousness does not grasp at its support to give rise to penetration, but merely contemplates the single thought-moment of the cognitive mind, whose essential nature is boundless and whose transformations are inexhaustible, thereby distancing oneself from the dependent nature and awakening to the perfected reality—is this perfect penetration? Or is it not?

Regarding the eighty-first question: The earth element is solid and obstructive, lacking penetration. Yet you say that even down to the nature of subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*), they do not touch one another.
If this is so, what is the difference between the nature of form being true emptiness and [the earth element]? By means of this, how does one enter the Way? [The answer is] perfect.

Question eighty-two: Regarding the Water Contemplation of the Youth Candraprabha, is it necessary to maintain focused mental recollection (*manasikāra*) before [attaining realization], or is there also a way to do so without adding such mental recollection?
As it is said: "The nature of water is true emptiness; the nature of emptiness is... [and so forth].
Pure and inherently luminous, pervading the entire Dharma-realm: is this perfect penetration? Is it not perfect penetration? (Question eighty-three):
When the supernormal power of the body experiences various tactile sensations of cold and heat, these are constantly present before one.
With the nature of fire being empty and true, pervading the entire Dharma-realm: is this perfect penetration? Is it not perfect penetration?
The eighty-fourth question: The Dharma Prince Vaidūryaprabha originally awakened to the wondrous clarity of fundamental enlightenment by perceiving immovability within movement.
At first, it seemed as though there were a counterpart; now that he has attained this, what further counterpart remains to be distinguished?
The eighty-fifth question: The Buddha who was the teacher of Vairocana-prabha was named Amitaghoṣa (Immeasurable Sound).

Is it not the case that sound, as a movement, is the counterpart to stillness? How does this differ from Avalokiteśvara’s awakening to the nature of hearing while confronted with the sense-object of sound?
The eighty-sixth question: Mañjuśrī refutes the nature of emptiness by challenging it on the grounds that it is merely dull and inert, rather than being awakened. [The response is:
If one contemplates that the nature is awakening and true emptiness, and that the nature is emptiness and true awakening—pure and fundamental from the beginning, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
Is it different from Bodhi? Is it not different? Is it complete penetration? Is it not complete penetration?

This is the eighty-seventh question. As for Maitreya Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the samādhi of mind-only consciousness and Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the ear-door samādhi—are they the same or different?
If they were the same, Mañjuśrī would not have singled out [Avalokiteśvara] to say, "Observe consciousness."
It is not permanent. If you say it is different, then consider the Samādhi of the Ear-Gate of Avalokiteśvara:

its fundamental observation is the essential clarity of consciousness, which is able to give rise to all conditions. That which is left behind by these conditions—namely, the essential clarity of consciousness—is what it is.
How does this differ from the perfect and true reality observed by Maitreya? Why, then, did Mañjuśrī insist on distinguishing between them?
Question Eighty-Eight: In the Bodhisattva Maitreya’s "Concentration on Mind-Only Consciousness" (*Cittamātra-vijñapti-samādhi*), which consciousness does he contemplate?

[The opponent] says it must be the *pariniṣpanna* (perfected) pure consciousness (*viśuddha-vijñāna*). Mañjuśrī should not have distinguished it by saying, "He contemplates that consciousness is not permanent," for [if it were the perfected nature], it would be non-delusory.
If he were contemplating a delusory consciousness subject to arising and ceasing, then Maitreya should not have said, "I, by means of... [and so forth].
"Only consciousness exists; the mind of consciousness is perfectly luminous, entering into the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

What does this mean? This is the eighty-ninth question. Those of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching all say: "One contemplates that the three realms are only mind, and all things are only consciousness."
Ninth and Tenth Questions: Is it the same or different to practice the *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only) samādhi together with Maitreya?

According to Maitreya’s own account, he contemplated the ten directions as consciousness-only; his cognitive mind became perfectly luminous, entering the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature), remaining far removed from the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) and the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature), thereby attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). He thus contemplated the ten directions.
"Representation-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*) refers first to the contemplation of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), which is itself the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

This corresponds to the preparatory application (*prayoga*) prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), wherein one performs the meditative concentration on the image-as-representation-only (*pratibimba-vijñapti-mātra-samādhi*).

Upon entering the perfected nature and becoming detached from the dependent nature and so forth, this is the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), wherein one performs the meditative concentration on reality-as-representation-only (*tattva-vijñapti-mātra-samādhi*). By analogy with this, the ear-gate samādhi of Avalokiteśvara is also...
There is the reality of reflected images; there are two kinds of certainty.
Question Ninety-one: Using the two Bodhisattvas Maitreya and Avalokiteśvara as examples, [this addresses] the Chan school’s direct pointing to the human mind.

Regarding "seeing one's nature to become a Buddha," when the Tiantai school contemplates the single thought-moment (*ekacitta*) to reveal, instruct, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*),
are there likewise two types— image and reality— and two levels of depth?
The ninety-second question: The Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta originally entered the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) by means of the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha.

Now, in this realm, he gathers those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha and leads them back to the Pure Land. Now, the patience of non-arising is the fruit, while mindfulness of the Buddha is the cause.
If the names of cause and fruit were not corresponding, how could one immediately enter the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas? If [the cause]...

If the fruit and its correspondence are thus, how does this differ from that of Avalokiteśvara? Yet Mañjuśrī has now disparaged it, claiming that all conditioned phenomena are by nature devoid of thought and fundamentally subject to arising and ceasing.
Since cause and effect are now so different, how can one attain perfect penetration through this?
Question Ninety-Third: Now, "mindfulness" (nian) is initial enlightenment (shijue), and "Buddha" is original enlightenment (benjue).

When the initial and the original mutually enter into the patience of non-arising (wusheng ren), how does this differ from Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva’s practice of "reversing the hearing to listen to one's own nature"?

Question Ninety-four: Regarding the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha, there are those who mindfully recollect the responsive Buddhas of other directions, and there are those who mindfully recollect the resultant Buddha within their own minds.
To mindfully recollect only the responsive Buddha of another direction—such as those today who single-mindedly recite the name of Amitābha—is to lose sight of one's own inherent power (*sva-bala*).

To mindfully recollect only the resultant Buddha of one’s own mind—such as those today who cultivate meditative concentration (*samādhi*) or engage in Chan meditation—is likewise to lose sight of [the Buddha].
This refers to relying on the power of others while losing one's own power; it is like a person who receives an official post through the protection of their ancestors.
It refers to losing the power of others while relying on one's own power; it is like a poor scholar who diligently masters the examination formats and succeeds in the civil service rankings.

If one relies on both, it is like inheriting an official post while simultaneously passing the formal examinations. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, with a mind of *nien-fo* (recollection of the Buddha), enters into non-existence.
This can be called the patience of birth, wherein one is mindful of both self and others. As Yongming said, "To possess both Chan and the Pure Land is like a tiger with horns;
how could this be inferior to Great Compassion? Yet why did Mañjuśrī insist on distinguishing between them?

The Ninety-Fifth Question: Generally, in the cultivation of perfect penetration, one does not go beyond causing each individual faculty to detach from its黏 *nian* (adhesive attachment) and settle inwardly.

As for the Venerable Lord of Great Compassion, he detached from the adhesive attachment solely through the gateway of the ear. As for the Venerable Lord of Great Power, he said, "I have no preference;
I gather all six faculties together to detach from the adhesive attachment. Regardless of whether one additionally attains the gateway of the ear, one shall transcend [the stages].
Question Ninety-six: Great Compassion encompasses all the sages; why then does Mañjuśrī not choose Mahāsthāmaprāpta, but instead chooses only Great Compassion?
Some say: "The faculty of hearing is most acute among the sentient beings of this region.

Since Great Compassion cultivated this very dharma during its causal stage, it shares a particularly abundant affinity with the sentient beings of Sahā. And as for the sentient beings of this region..."

As for those who, being born [in this world], exclusively revere, serve, and invoke the name of Avalokiteśvara—it is for this reason that even now there are many sentient beings who have a particular affinity for Amitābha and extensively revere, serve, and invoke his name.
How could the Dharma-gate of the Great Power (Mahāsthāmaprāpta) not be equal to the Great Compassionate One? Why then does Mañjuśrī extol one while disparaging the other?

The ninety-seventh question: Regarding what is called "cultivating the gate of the ear" by Jiaoguang—taking only the essence without divisions and entering directly with a single blade—there are indeed those of sharp faculties who, upon a single entry, enter forever and immediately attain the manifestation of quiescence.
Yet there are also those of middling or inferior capacities who do not immediately enter; because their defiled habits are particularly heavy, they must still rely on other gates.
Is it so? Or is it not so? Question Ninety-Eight:
Before the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* had reached China, did the eminent monks of this land in ancient times also enter the Way through various other gates? Yes or no?

Question One Hundred and Eight: Because one returns to the source, the gates are established; having returned to the source, one rejoices in the gates.
Once the feet have crossed the threshold, there are a thousand differences; once the feet have just entered the portal, there is profound identity. By means of the manifold, all is unified;
by means of the one, all is [unified]. Is this so? Or is it not so?
The ocean of meaning of the two sutras and the heart-essence of the patriarchs—this single drop of water circulates without end.
Consequently, though difficult questions and billions of inquiries might never be exhausted, I have ceased at one hundred and eight merely to avoid excessive prolixity.
Nevertheless, as these all concern the locus of principle, I have recorded them as they came to my lips and noted them with my hand, without initially deliberating on their beginning or end.
If one were to answer each point regarding this meaning, it would accord with the *Lengyan jing hejie* (Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra) by the Dharma Master Jiaoguang.
